ci: report how many runner minutes came from paid capacity
metricHints: `ci-health-report.yml` runs four times a day and totals runner minutes by label. Every label renders the same way, so nothing in the report distinguishes free capacity from billed capacity:
- **Blacksmith** and **GitHub-hosted** are free to this repository.
- **WarpBuild** is metered per minute, at roughly double the rate on its 12-vCPU labels.
A lane that drifts onto paid capacity therefore reads as an ordinary row in the existing tables, and the drift stays invisible until somebody reads an invoice.

Because `runs-on` sends pull requests through `MACOS_RUNNER_PR` and everything else through `MACOS_RUNNER_15`, the practical effect is that **pull requests run free while main and the merge queue run metered** — and neither gate validates the other's pool.

**Paid runner capacity (WarpBuild):** none in the window.

- `python3 scripts/ci/run_python_test_lane.py --lane linux-guard` — exit 0.

records.title: test(simulator): bound the panel waits by a deadline, not a yield count
metricHints: The waits in these two files spun a fixed yield count before asserting:

A yield count is not a deadline. `Task.yield()` gives the scheduler a chance to run something else; it does not wait for anything. So 100 yields is however long 100 reschedules happen to take — microseconds on an idle machine, and unrelated to how long the awaited work actually needs. The bound tightens exactly when the runner is busy, which is the shape ...

Ten polls across `SimulatorPanelIntegrationTests` and `SimulatorPanelThemeTests` now bound the same predicate with a `ContinuousClock` deadline instead. They still return the instant the condition holds, so a passing run is no slower; only a genuinely broken one waits out the 10 s. No assertion changed, and no test's meaning changed.

The two bare `for _ in 0..<100 { await Task.yield() }` at `SimulatorPanelIntegrationTests.swift:187` and `:252` assert an **absence** (`discoveryCount == 0`, `!isCompleted`). A deadline cannot bound a wait for a non-event — the fix there is a positive completion signal to assert after, which changes what the test observes rather than how long it waits, an...

**These tests require a macOS runner, which I do not have — CI here is their first execution.** A green shard is the evidence that matters; parse-level checks do not establish that the converted polls still observe what they used to.

records.title: ci(ios): bound the xcodebuild test invocation so a teardown wedge fails fast
metricHints: In run [35823476668](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux/actions/runs/35823476668) both `ios-simulator` legs finished their tests in about two minutes, then emitted nothing for 32m45s and were killed by `timeout-minutes: 35`.
xctest wedges *after* the run rather than during it: its last line is a suite result, it never emits the `Test run with N tests` summary, and at 05:50:16 it logs

— waiting on a termination for a process that is already gone. `xcodebuild` is still alive at kill time; the runner's orphan sweep has to terminate it (`pid 1740 (xcodebuild)`, `pid 1791 (DTServiceHub)`).

The invocation had no bound of its own, so the 35-minute job ceiling was the only one. That is **71 macOS runner-minutes per occurrence for no added signal**, and it is invisible: a `timeout-minutes` expiry reports as `conclusion: cancelled`, not `failure`, so the job never appears in a census of failing jobs and reads like an ordinary supersession.
- selected tests passed, bad exit → tolerated as a runner cleanup failure, job green
So the run above would have reported its five `TerminalViewportSpacingTests` assertion failures in about three minutes, as a `failure`, instead of being `cancelled` at thirty-five.

900s is generous against the ~2 minutes the non-UI suite actually takes and low enough against the 35-minute ceiling to leave the later steps room. A wedge does not match the loop's retry greps, so it consumes one attempt rather than two.

The lane was gated shut until an hour ago: #13886 made `ios-simulator` require `package-conventions-lint`, which was red on `main` (#10409), so runs stopped before the simulator legs. #13904 fixed the lint. Multiple filters share the one build and run in one test job: measured test execution is ~15 s median, so a job-per-filter would pay a product download and app-host setup per selector to parallelize seconds of work.

**Stated plainly: for a single fresh dispatch this does not reduce total runner minutes.** It adds a second runner's checkout and setup plus an artifact round trip, against a compile it does not yet avoid. The win today is reruns and the cheap early filter; the large win needs cross-run adoption, which this PR deliberately does not attempt.

records.title: ci: default focused E2E dispatches to macOS 26
metricHints: A focused dispatch that does not name a runner waits a median 2.4 minutes to start, and a p90 of 83 minutes. `test-e2e.yml`'s `auto` resolves to `vars.MACOS_RUNNER_TESTS || 'blacksmith-6vcpu-macos-15'`, and **that repository variable is not set**, so every such dispatch lands on the macOS 15 pool's queue.

`auto` falls back to `blacksmith-6vcpu-macos-26`. Setting `MACOS_RUNNER_TESTS` still overrides it, and `--runner blacksmith-6vcpu-macos-15` still reaches the old pool for questions that are specifically about macOS 15. `skills/cmux-testing` says so and says to expect the wait.
## Before / after
| queue median | 2.4 min | **0.3 min** |
| queue p90 | 83.3 min | **1.0 min** |
| queue max | 177.7 min | **1.4 min** |
| execution median | **18.7 min** | 22.5 min |
| total elapsed median | 26.8 min | **23.0 min** |

**The tradeoff runs the other way on execution:** macOS 26 ran about 4 min slower per job, so this buys wall-clock and predictability at a small cost in runner minutes. Total elapsed still favors 26 once queueing is counted. I have not isolated why execution differs — the two groups are not the same tests, so treat that column as observed, not causal.

This is not a leap: 25 of the 60 dispatches in the window already ran on macOS 26 and concluded normally (9 success, 11 failure, 5 cancelled). `scripts/select-ci-xcode.sh` picks by SDK with the lane's existing `CMUX_CI_MAX_MACOS_SDK_MAJOR: "26"` ceiling and falls back on older runners, so neither pool needs an Xcode pin.
The SPM cache key includes the resolved runner, so macOS 26 starts on its own cache namespace and the first dispatches there will miss it.

`tests/test_ci_self_hosted_guard.sh` pinned the literal `blacksmith-6vcpu-macos-15` inside its **Tart canary identity** check, so changing a default failed an assertion about something unrelated. That check's subject is the effective-runner expression, not which macOS generation it falls back to, so it now matches the shape (`blacksmith-6vcpu-macos-[0-9]+...

Changes the default runner for focused E2E dispatches from `blacksmith-6vcpu-macos-15` to `blacksmith-6vcpu-macos-26` to escape the macOS 15 pool's long queue times (2.4 min median, 83.3 min p90 vs 0.3 min / 1.0 min on macOS 26).
- Setting `MACOS_RUNNER_TESTS` still overrides the default, and `--runner blacksmith-6vcpu-macos-15` still targets the old pool explicitly.
- macOS 26 executes about 4 min slower per job (22.5 vs 18.7 min median), but total elapsed still favors it (23.0 vs 26.8 min) once queueing is counted.
- The SPM cache key includes the resolved runner, so the first macOS 26 runs start with a cold cache.

records.title: ci: reuse an in-flight focused run instead of dispatching over it
metricHints: `scripts/run-e2e.sh` refuses a selector that already failed at a commit, but says nothing about one that is still queued or running. Dispatching there is worse than a repeat: `test-e2e.yml`'s concurrency group is keyed on runner, ref and the whole `test_filter` string with `cancel-in-progress: true`, so an identical dispatch cancels the run that is alread...
- **attaches** to an identical in-flight run — same commit, same selector set, **same runner** — printing its URL and watching it under `--wait`, instead of dispatching;

- **refuses** a selector already in flight on that pool under a *different* batch. That batch does not share the concurrency group, so it would not cancel anything; it would pay a second full compile of identical source to answer a question already running.
## Before / after
| | before | after |
| identical dispatch while one is in flight | cancels the running compile, restarts cold | prints and watches the running one, no runner spent |
| overlapping batch at the same ref | second full compile | refused, names the live run |

Measured against this exact artifact from a laptop: 39 s vs. a single stream that was on pace for ~90 s on the same link, and the runner's single...

It is wired as `Try parallel GitHub artifact transport` in both consumers, after the node-local, peer, selective-layer and R2 sources. `scripts/ci/app_host_layer_transport.py` uses the same helper for each pinned layer ZIP, so #13567's "fewer bytes" and this "faster bytes" compose (diagnostics, the layer that selective restore skips, is ~21% of the produc...

records.title: test: bound SSH fish helper pipe draining
metricHints: The SSH/fish integration test waits for its child before reading stdout/stderr. A child that fills either pipe can block before exiting; an inherited writer can also keep EOF open after the direct child exits. This PR drains both pipes concurrently and bounds the post-exit drain at two seconds, retaining stderr for failure diagnosis.
- A background child retaining the pipe writers for 15 seconds must not delay the direct child's result until EOF. The fixture cleans up that child afterward.

This PR does not add a separate workflow gate or change shard packing, retries, runner size, or production app behavior. Earlier descriptions of a dedicated SSH/fish tail gate do not describe the current diff.

records.title: test(warm-slot): rendezvous with the child instead of sleeping 50 ms
metricHints: `test_forced_kill_still_requires_observed_process_group_settlement` asks for preemption 50 ms after launching a child that is supposed to ignore `SIGTERM`:

The child only ignores `SIGTERM` once `signal.signal(...)` has run. If Python interpreter startup loses that 50 ms race, `SIGTERM` takes its default action, the child is gone well inside the patched `TERM_GRACE_SECONDS = 0.01`, `force_after_grace` returns early without killing anything, and `force_killed` is `False`.

I found it sweeping all 106 `linux-guard` tests against `main` locally. It is green in CI today, so this is a latent flake rather than a live break — the kind that costs a rerun of a whole guard lane when the runner happens to be slow.

The child creates a FIFO after installing its handler; the requesting thread blocks on opening it. A FIFO open rendezvouses both ends, so there is no polling and no sleep — the preemption simply cannot be requested before the handler exists.

Fixes a race in `test_forced_kill_still_requires_observed_process_group_settlement` where the 50 ms sleep could beat interpreter startup, letting the default `SIGTERM` action kill the child inside the term grace and flakily fail the `force_killed` assertion.

The child now opens a FIFO after installing its handler, and the requesting thread blocks on opening it, so preemption cannot be requested before the handler exists. The thread runs as a daemon so a child that never reaches the rendezvous fails the assertions instead of wedging the suite on a blocked `open()`.

records.title: ci: seed the test compilation cache from one clean build
metricHints: `refresh-test-compilation-cache` restored its own last seed by prefix before rebuilding, so every scheduled run stacked another build's objects onto one CAS. Xcode keeps the primary generation and the upstream it faults objects in from, and that pair grew until it crossed the 5 GiB save bound today:
| 09-22 12:38 | 5,027,256 KiB | last run that saved |
| 09-22 18:33 | **5,293,516 KiB** | over the 5,242,880 KiB bound, save skipped |
Past the bound the save step is skipped, so the next run restores the same older entry and lands past the bound again. `nightly.yml` already documents that state for the Release seed:
> Nothing is saved, so the next build restores the same older entry and lands here again: the cache freezes at its last saved entry until the bound (and `COMPILATION_CACHE_LIMIT_SIZE`) is raised.
- **Bounded.** 3.5 GiB, so the bound stops being reachable instead of being raised.
- **Faster to produce.** The one cold run took 18 min; the warm ones took 19, 19, 21 and 25.
- **Faster to consume.** Every pull request restores this entry, so it is ~1.5 GiB less to download on each one.
- `tests/test_ci_test_compilation_cache_seed.sh` fails on the first commit, passes on the second.

Independent, and both are needed. #13754 makes the seed *reachable* by a pull request at all; this makes it keep *updating*. #13754 also resets the size ratchet as a side effect, because a new runner means a new fingerprint and so the first run finds no prefix to stack on — but without this change the ratchet would just climb back to the bound and freeze ...

Stops the test compilation cache seed from growing past the 5 GiB save bound and freezing at its last saved entry. The seeder restored its own last seed by prefix, so each scheduled run stacked another build's objects onto the CAS until it crossed the bound, at which point saving was skipped and the cache could no longer update.
Seeding from one clean build keeps the cache bounded and current: 3.5 GiB instead of 5.0 GiB, covers all of main, and takes 18 min to produce instead of 19–25.

records.title: fix(ci): bound Glaeda cache growth on the persistent Mac
metricHints: Glaeda does not clean up after itself. Its own `docs/APPLE_NATIVE_BUILDS.md` is explicit:
> Old generations are retained for inspection; this prototype performs no automatic eviction or broad cache cleanup. Disk use can therefore grow after toolchain/configuration changes.

Each generation holds a full cmux DerivedData tree, and the cache key changes with the toolchain. So every Xcode or SDK bump stranded a multi-GB directory on the owned Mac permanently — on a fleet where, per `docs/ci-runners.md`, "hosts reject new jobs below their free-space threshold". Unbounded growth on a machine that refuses work when full eventually ...

After a verified compile, stamp the generation this run used and evict all but the three most recently used. Retention covers a toolchain bump plus a rollback onto the previous generation without forcing a cold rebuild, while bounding disk to three DerivedData trees.

- **Only after the compile is proven.** Pruning runs after the build succeeds *and* after every existing check on the current generation's locator (cache root containment, DerivedData containment, build log and products present). A failed run never deletes on the strength of an unvalidated plan. Enforced by a test asserting the call site sits after each o...

- **Ordering is an explicit stamp, not incidental mtime.** `main` calls `os.utime(resolved_cache)` on the generation it just used, immediately before pruning. This matters: Xcode's writes land under `derived_data/` and do not update the generation directory's own mtime, so without the stamp a long-lived warm generation could look *older* than a cold one a...
- plus a call-site test pinning eviction after the compile guards and after the `os.utime` stamp.
python3 tests/test_ci_persistent_mac_compile.py -> Ran 22 tests, OK  (16 before)

Bounds unbounded disk growth on the persistent Mac CI runner. Glaeda never evicts its own cache generations and each one holds a full cmux DerivedData tree, so every Xcode or SDK bump stranded a multi-GB directory on a host that rejects jobs below its free-space threshold.
After a verified compile, the driver stamps the generation it used and deletes all but the three most recently used. Eviction is deliberately conservative:
- Pruning runs only after the compile succeeds and every locator guard passes.
* Cache cleanup now occurs only after successful compilation, preventing failed runs from removing valid cache data.

records.title: fix(ios): assign a delivered TestFlight build even if a later step fails
metricHints: All of them run after Apple has accepted the build. `assign-internal-group` gated on `needs.upload.result == 'success'`, so a failure in any of them skipped it: **the build reached App Store Connect and then reached nobody.** The run goes red pointing at "Upload to TestFlight", which is the one thing that did work.
- `!cancelled()` is load-bearing, not decoration: a failed `needs` skips a job **before** its `if` is evaluated, so without it the outputs gate could never become true.
- A job that fails *before* the upload step leaves `steps.upload.outcome` empty, so the gate is false and assignment is correctly skipped. Only a delivered IPA opens it.
- `final_build_number`, `bundle_id` and `assign_internal_group` all come from steps that ran before the upload step, so a later failure leaves them populated.

It also asserts **the hazard itself** — that steps still run after `id: upload` — so if the post-upload work is ever moved out of the job, the guard says so rather than passing vacuously. It parses the workflow as text rather than with PyYAML, matching the other `release-ios` guards, because that matrix group installs no Python packages.

Fixes TestFlight builds being left unassigned when a step after the upload fails. The `assign-internal-group` job previously gated on the whole upload job's result, so a failure in any of the four steps that run after Apple accepts the build skipped assignment and left the delivered build in App Store Connect assigned to nobody.
* Added automated coverage to verify TestFlight assignment behavior after post-upload failures.

The router attaches at `requested` instead. Attaching at `requested` means the router starts before CI has begun a job, so the wait for the route request artifact now has to span CI's queue time as well as the `changes` job that publishes it. Two changes keep that bounded:
- the deadline grows from 180 to 600 seconds, and the poll interval from 2 to 5 seconds;

- the job budget grows from 15 to 25 minutes. 15 was sized for the 180s wait; a 600s wait plus a dispatch that `persistent_mac_route.py` admits up to 600s of queue and execution for does not fit, and being killed after dispatch could leave an owned Mac compiling for a run nobody reads;

- the route job's condition now excludes forks via `head_repository.full_name`, which `requested` populates, so a fork no longer holds a runner for 600s to learn what the request envelope already requires;

- the wait ends early, after one final look for the artifact, once the CI run has reached `completed` without publishing one. The common case is a run superseded by a new push, which `cancel-in-progress` cancels within seconds; that run now releases the router's runner instead of idling to the deadline. records.title: Bound warm-slot telemetry without per-event fsync
metricHints: - Bound retention to `events.jsonl` plus one 16 MiB archive at `events.jsonl.1`.
- Repair one crash-torn JSONL tail before the next append; archive-only restart states recreate the current journal.

There is no telemetry writer thread or shutdown drain. Each call holds `events.lock` through tail repair/rotation/append and closes its descriptor before returning, so shutdown and rotation have no queue race.
| metric | before | after | reduction |
| p50 event append | 0.0698 ms | 0.0592 ms | 15.2% |
| p95 event append | 0.1438 ms | 0.1002 ms | 30.3% |
| mean event append | 0.0847 ms | 0.0672 ms | 20.7% |
| median 500-event batch | 43.74 ms | 33.42 ms | 23.6% |
| event-journal fsyncs/event | 1 | 0 | 100% |
| event-journal appends/event | 1 | 1 | 0% |

The overlay filesystem makes `fsync` unusually cheap, so the latency delta understates the persistent-storage savings. The deterministic write reduction is one durability barrier removed from every telemetry event.
Fixes #13533. Bounds warm-slot event telemetry to one current journal plus one 16 MiB archive and removes the durability barrier from every event, cutting benchmark append latency by roughly 15–30%.

- Rotates with `os.replace()` under `events.lock`, repairs a crash-torn JSONL tail before the next append, and recreates the current journal when only the archive survives a restart. There is no writer thread or shutdown drain.

metricHints: - After `xcodebuild`, every `reload.sh` run re-copies the app to the tag-named bundle, rewrites its `Info.plist`, rebuilds/installs helpers and re-signs, even when nothing changed. This records a per-tag receipt (`/.cmux-reload/`) of the inputs to that post-build work and skips it when the inputs and the tagged app are unchanged.

- The reuse key includes a fingerprint of **the app `xcodebuild` just produced**: its `Info.plist`, its code-signing seal (`_CodeSignature/CodeResources`, which covers every resource in the bundle) and its executables under `Contents/MacOS` and `Contents/Resources/bin`. Costs about 0.1 s. It replaces the first version's `git diff` key, which was empty aft...
- Before reusing, the tagged app's signature is verified and its `Info.plist` is checked, so a deleted or damaged bundle is rebuilt.

Measured on one machine (MacBook Air M5, Xcode 27.0), before = #13022's head, after = this branch, same warm DerivedData, same tag, `reload.sh --tag … --no-global-cli-links`, both with #12973 merged locally so `reload.sh` runs outside the shared dev backend. Compare within a row only.
| step | before | after | tagged app reused | tagged executable hash |
| warm no-op reload, 3 runs | 22.5 / 20.2 / 20.8 s | **10.4 to 12.9 s** (7 runs) | yes | unchanged |
| **committed** one-line edit in an app-target Swift file | | 55.2 s | **no** | changed |
| one-line **code** edit in a local package (uncommitted) | | 27.5 s | **no** | changed |
| uncommitted one-line edit in an app-target Swift file | | 46.0 s | no | changed |
| tagged app bundle deleted | | 21.8 s, bundle re-created | no | |
| tagged app `Info.plist` corrupted | | 20.5 s, plist valid again, `codesign --verify --deep` passes | no | |
- Stores per-tag receipts under `/.cmux-reload/` and verifies the tagged app's signature and `Info.plist` before reusing it.

records.title: ci: drop a stalled GhosttyKit download and resume it
metricHints: A `macOS compile admission` job (https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux/actions/runs/35505026493/job/106063760947) spent its whole life in "Download pre-built GhosttyKit.xcframework": 123 MB at about 70 KB/s, while the sibling job in the same run fetched it in 4 s. The script could not recover:
- curl's built-in `--retry` starts the output file over, so every attempt needed 410 KB/s to finish and none could. With 30 retries that is hours of a paid Mac doing nothing.

Now a connection under 256 KB/s for 15 s is dropped, and the retry loop runs one curl process per attempt with `--continue-at -`, so progress is kept and the next connection usually lands on a healthy path. If the server refuses the range, the partial file is discarded. The pinned SHA-256 check is unchanged and still decides whether the file is accepted.

Fixes stalled GhosttyKit downloads in CI so a slow transfer no longer waits out the 300s cap and restarts from zero. A connection that stays under 256 KB/s for 15 s is now dropped, and retries keep partial progress.

metricHints: Retargeted to main after https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux/pull/13160 merged. The repository is provisioned and `CI_CACHE_BACKEND=r2` is set; R2 takes effect when this lands.
- Adds a third cache store to the `cache-restore` and `cache-save` actions: an R2 bucket, selected with `CI_CACHE_BACKEND=r2` or the `cache_backend` dispatch input.

- Why: the Warp store is only reachable from Warp runners and the Blacksmith store only from Blacksmith runners, so moving providers (or running two, or fork pull requests falling back to another provider) starts from empty seeds. R2 is reachable from every runner, has no size cap and no egress fee, and cache writes use a dedicated bucket-scoped token, se...

- Saves (`scripts/ci/r2-cache.sh save`) run only in the `nightly.yml` seed jobs and the nightly app build. They sign with `curl --aws-sigv4`, upload the archive, then write one small pointer per dash-terminated key prefix, pointers last. The bucket credentials are empty in the step env unless that run saves to R2, and `ci.yml` never references them.
- Archives are zstd when the runner has `zstd`, gzip otherwise; restore accepts either.
A lifecycle rule deleting objects older than about 14 days keeps it small; seeds are about 2 GB per seed run.

Provisioned: `cmux-ci-cache`, public URL `https://ci-cache.cmux.com`, TLS 1.2 minimum, 14-day object expiry and 1-day incomplete-upload expiry. The dedicated `CI_CACHE_R2_*` secrets are installed. The shared release `CF_R2_*` secrets are unchanged. Anonymous PUT is denied and the cache credential cannot access `cmux-binaries`.

- `tests/test_ci_r2_cache.sh` runs the script against a local object server: miss on an empty store, save uploads the archive and every prefix pointer, exact restore reports a hit with identical files, prefix restore names the matched key without claiming a hit, an existing key is not re-saved, a pointer naming a key outside its prefix is ignored, a corru...

- Real Mac measurements (unchanged app sources): [cold run](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux/actions/runs/35500307901), [warm run](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux/actions/runs/35501759139). Cold build 29m00s, job 33m12s; warm build 3m54s, job 7m28s. Warm restores: compilation cache 24s, packages 16s, with no `Cache miss` lines in the warm build log...

- R2 save time was 64s per cold archive, 54s for the warm compilation archive. The earlier Warp reference reported 19s and 16s saves and 40s combined restores. R2 storage is cheaper and restore time is comparable; total runner-cost savings are not established because uploads take longer.

- [Manual Debug/Release seeding](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux/actions/runs/35501760164) passed; app build, signing, and publishing jobs were skipped as intended. The Debug compilation archive is 658 MB and uploaded successfully.

Adds an optional R2 cache store that every runner provider can read, so caches no longer start empty when work moves between providers or runs as a fork pull request. It is off by default, and `nightly.yml` can now seed it manually without building or publishing an app.
- Restores download from a public read-only URL, so they need no credentials and work on any runner and on fork pull requests.
- Pointer writes are conditional and keyed to the run number, so older runs cannot overwrite newer pointers and a failed pointer is repaired on the next save without re-uploading its archive.
- Archives are zstd when the runner has it, gzip otherwise; restore accepts either, and zstd restores consume trailing tar padding so macOS `bsdtar` cannot turn a valid restore into a miss.
* Added R2 as a cache backend for restoring and saving CI caches.

metricHints: `macos-compile-admission` compiles the app-host test product from an empty compilation cache on every run (about 800 s). - **Fingerprint in the key:** the script's `fingerprint` command hashes `xcodebuild -version`, the workspace path and the DerivedData path. Blacksmith checks out under `/Users/runner/_work`, Warp under `/Users/runner/work`, and fork PRs land on Warp because repository variables are not exposed to them. A seed from the other layout misses every path-bearin...

Why scheduled and not on every push to `main`: Swift invalidates a whole module when one file in it changes. In the admission log for run 35421373371, all ~98 package targets finish in the first ~135 s, then `cmux` takes ~340 s and `cmuxTests` ~180 s. A PR that touches `Sources/` recompiles `cmux` and `cmuxTests` whatever the seed holds, so what the seed ...

Why PRs do not save: a cache written from a PR is scoped to that PR. It helps no other PR and spends the shared cache budget (Blacksmith documents 25 GB per repo per week, LRU) that keeps the main seed alive.
| no cache | 953 s | |
| nothing edited | 157 s | 0 misses |
| a comment line appended to one package file | 152 s | 28 misses, app target fully cached |
| an app-target file edited | 697 s | app target misses entirely, packages hit |

The Release seed shows the same shape in CI: a pull request with no Swift changes replayed 1116 hits / 0 misses in 6 min; one that touched `CMUXMobileCore` had 1074 hits / 52 misses and took 33 min, because the misses were the large modules.

- Mutation check: the guard fails when the PR job is switched to a saving `actions/cache`, when the seeder's key prefix or CAS path drifts, when the script drops `build-for-testing` or `COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_CACHING`, and when the seeder is moved to `push`.

- The seeder cannot run until this is on `main` (schedule only), so the hit rate above is a prediction from the Release seed's behaviour, not a measurement. After the first scheduled run, an admission log's `Cache hit` / `Cache miss` counts will settle it.

- https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux/pull/13046 (PathKit) is not needed here because the seed and the reader build from identical paths. It would matter if CI turned on prefix mapping to share one seed across runner layouts.

records.title: ci: skip blocked internal TestFlight polls
metricHints: Internal TestFlight polls currently wait up to five hours for earlier uploads, and every waiting poll re-checks the workflow queue once a minute. When an upload is delayed, this creates a growing number of API requests and can exhaust the repository’s `GITHUB_TOKEN` rate limit.

This change makes the 20-minute internal poll idempotent: if an earlier upload is still running or ordering cannot be inspected, the poll records `should_build=false`, exits, and lets the next poll retry. Manual dispatches and the twice-daily DEMO schedule keep the existing wait behavior.

records.title: ci: stop routing workflow plumbing changes to macOS
metricHints: 3. **A `ci.yml` edit confined to Linux jobs is neutral.** The routing step hands the detector the base `ci.yml` and it compares the two job by job. macOS is skipped only when the text before `jobs:` (triggers, env, permissions, concurrency) is unchanged, every changed, added or removed job plainly runs on Linux in both revisions, and neither `changes` nor...
